abstract: Several countries are working to interlink their domestic fast payment systems in order to reduce costs and improve the speed and transparency of cross-border payments. This column presents econometric evidence suggesting that countries with interlinked systems trade with each other about 4% more than countries that lack such interlinkages. The trade gains are larger in regions with high cross-border payment costs and for systems that allow the settlement of wholesale transactions.
authors: Massimo Ferrari Minesso, Laura Lebastard, Olga Triay Bagur

abstract: The expansion of artificial intelligence has triggered a surge of investment and rising equity values at technology firms. The largest firms, known as ‘hyperscalers’, issued over $100 billion of bonds in 2025, around five times the 2023-2024 annual average. This column compares bond yields for hyperscalers and other firms, before and after ChatGPT’s release in 2022. Hyperscalers’ yields fell by about 29 basis points relative to other firms, and by 42 basis points relative to software firms, whose business models artificial intelligence may disrupt. As hyperscalers’ debt grows, it remains critical to monitor whether these pricing effects continue.
title: Financing the AI boom: Winners and losers in corporate bond markets

abstract: This paper introduces a ranking over opportunity sets based on preferences satisficing: a set satisfices a preference if and only if there exists an element in the set that is considered good enough to meet the preference, and sets are ranked by the number of satisficed preferences. I compare this framework with existing models of ranking over sets and show that, when preferences are not exogenously given, it is characterized by two axioms identical to those in Kreps (1979), who analyzed rankings over sets from the perspective of preferences maximization. This result indicates that we cannot distinguish whether the ranking over sets is generated according to preferences maximization or preferences satisficing.
title: Diversity in opportunity sets: perspective from preferences satisficing

abstract: Developing countries face critical tensions between farmland-use policies prioritizing food security and environmental sustainability, and farmers’ livelihood-centered land-use strategies. To address these challenges, this study develops a human-centered agent-based model that integrates dual-layer Q-learning with GIS-based spatial representation. This framework simulates farmers’ adaptive decision-making under dynamic policy and environmental conditions while formalizing behavioral heterogeneity through Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB)-informed typologies. Agents dynamically evolve land-transfer and cropping strategies via perception–action–feedback learning cycles. Applied to and validated against empirical observations from a representative Chinese case, the model reveals non-linear scale–efficiency relationships, with medium-scale farms exhibiting the comparatively balanced performance across yield and multiple resource-use efficiency dimensions. The analysis further identifies evolutionary pathways of adaptive behavior under policy incentives and quantifies trade-offs among area-weighted crop output, resource-use efficiency, and regional gross income. Scenario simulations show that rice-oriented subsidies increase rice output but reduce resource-use efficiency, rapeseed output, and gross income, whereas rotation-oriented incentives increase gross income while maintaining rice output near the baseline level. These findings support performance-linked subsidies based on multidimensional outcomes, tiered land-transfer regulation, and diversified cropping incentives. By linking adaptive behavioral dynamics with spatial and institutional constraints, this study provides a robust analytical framework for evaluating land-use policies and supports more effective governance strategies for balancing food security, environmental sustainability, and rural livelihoods.
